newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia plans jumbo mark Eurobond in March.
newsitem.headline: Russia plans jumbo mark Eurobond in March.

text.p: Russia will follow up last November's successful Eurobond debut with another offering in marks next month, a senior finance ministry official said on Monday.

Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov told Reuters the new bond, for about one billion marks, would be issued in March through Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and CS First Boston, after last year's $1 billion Eurobond was highly oversubscribed.
"This issue is mainly aimed at investors in Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Benelux countries," he said.

November's bond, marking Russia's return to world capital markets for the first time since the 1917 Bolshevik revolution was the biggest ever debut Eurobond and showed Moscow that there was massive demand for its debt.
Kasyanov said Russia would raise a total of $3 billion in Eurobonds this year, with two or three issues in various currencies.
The first Eurobond was priced to yield only 3.45 percentage points more than U.S. Treasury bonds, much less than Western bankers originally thought Moscow would have to pay.
Kasyanov said he thought the new mark Eurobond would pay a similar spread over U.S. Treasuries of around 350 basis points.
News of the new bond was welcomed in the market for Russia's dollar-denominated MinFin bonds, where prices rose by up to one percentage point.
"The market opened high and now it is rising on the news about our mark Eurobond," an Aljba-Alliance dealer said.
Dealers said foreign investors, who have already driven Russian shares to record levels this year, appeared no longer to be worried by President Boris Yeltsin's poor health.
"Everyone has got accustomed to that," said a Moscow Narodny Bank dealer in London.
The market was encouraged by comments from French President Jacques Chirac, who visited Yeltsin on Sunday, that he was impressed at the speed of Yeltsin's recovery.
Yeltsin is recovering from pneumonia and underwent multiple heart bypass surgery last November.
Dealers said foreign investors were looking more at recent progress in restructuring the Russian economy rather than at political problems.

The authorities have managed to stabilise the rouble over the last 18 months and bring annual inflation to less than 22 percent. They have also nearly finished rescheduling much of the huge debts inherited from the former Soviet Union.

Kasyanov said Russia and the London Club of commercial bank creditors would close their multi-billion dollar debt rescheduling at the end of March or start of April, when the long and tortuous work of reconciling individual loans with hundreds of banks was finally over.
Rescheduling the $35 billion in debts and interest arrears owed the London Club will close a four-year saga between Russia and more than 3,000 lenders.
Russia has also reached agreements on rescheduling the $40 billion it owes the Paris Club of government creditors and over $5 billion in uninsured debt owed to commercial companies.
The Moscow Narodny MinFin dealer said the market was not discouraged by news that the closing of the London Club reschedulig may take until April instead of the end of March, as previously announced.
"Everyone understands the debt is huge and complicated, it could not have been closed so quickly," he said.
